lesson_title: Four Storeys of Sky: the Structure of the Atmosphere
hook_text: The sky is a block of flats with the heaters in the wrong places.
clip_script: Picture the sky as a block of flats, four storeys high, with heating that makes no sense until you know where the heaters are. Ground floor — the troposphere. The heater is the FLOOR: the ground soaks up sunshine and radiates it upward, so the higher you climb, the colder it gets. That is why the Drakensberg carries snow on a day Durban is swimming weather. All the weather lives on this floor. First floor — the stratosphere. Now the heater is on the CEILING: ozone catches ultraviolet and turns it into warmth, so it gets warmer as you climb. Warm air on top of cool air is a lid — nothing rises, no clouds form. That is why aeroplanes fly here. Second floor — the mesosphere. No heater at all: the coldest place in the whole building, around minus ninety, where shooting stars burn up. Top floor — the thermosphere. Thousands of degrees on the thermometer, and you would still freeze, because there is almost no air up there to touch you. Four floors. Down, up, down, up.
visual_style: A cutaway block of flats dissolving into a real sky column, each storey lighting up with its heater glowing in a different place, a zigzag temperature line drawing itself up the side.
mood: Playful architecture turning into genuine awe.
pacing: One clean beat per storey, quickening through the last two, landing hard on 'down, up, down, up'.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read the atmosphere's temperature graph without memorising a single height.
